item_name: STRAIGHT-IN (FLAPS LDG, FLAPS UP, FLAPS Τ/Ο).

texts.0: SP, due to a late power reduction and an unstabilized pitch/power relationship, did not regulate the final approach airspeed within the one-sided tolerance of the effective landing pattern. Airspeed exceeded the computed final speed by more than 15 knots inside 2 NM and at a later point decayed below the computed value, which the criteria do not permit at all. IP had to direct power and pitch corrections, and the approach was never stabilized on speed before the threshold.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed pitch/power correction after the configuration change, allowed the final approach airspeed to reach the +15 knot limit of the tolerance. SP reduced power only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP and the computed speed was re-established late on final. No control input by the IP was required, but the airspeed was regulated by instruction rather than by SP's own cross-check of the airspeed indicator.
texts.2: SP, due to a high power setting carried through the configuration change, allowed the final approach airspeed to increase past +10 knots above the computed value. SP identified the trend on the airspeed indicator, reduced power in time and contained the excursion short of the +15 knot limit, restoring the computed speed before short final. No prompting or intervention by the IP was needed.
texts.3: SP flew the final at the computed approach airspeed and held the deviation within +10, -0 knots throughout the approach. SP adjusted power promptly at each configuration change and at no point allowed the speed to decay below the computed value. Airspeed remained stable from the configuration point to the threshold.
texts.4: SP established the computed final approach airspeed immediately after configuring and held it to the threshold with negligible deviation. Power corrections were small and anticipatory, and the speed never approached the lower boundary of the tolerance. Airspeed control was maintained without any prompting at any stage of the approach.
texts.marginal: SP kept the final approach airspeed inside standards, but the deviation stayed consistently in the upper part of the band and required a further power reduction on short final on each approach. The tendency is to carry excess power through the configuration change and to correct reactively instead of anticipating the speed loss. SP is expected to set the target power earlier so that the computed airspeed is established before 2 NM.

texts_at.0: SP flew the final approach airspeed control, with the IP demonstrating the technique first, a first exposure to this task at this stage of the syllabus. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard, and SP is expected to carry more of the task independently at the next opportunity.
texts_at.1: SP held the final approach airspeed inside the code 1 band, reaching about 14 knots above the computed value after a momentarily high power setting carried through the configuration change. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to retard power sooner after the change so the margin below the 15 knot limit grows.
texts_at.2: SP held the final approach airspeed inside the code 2 band, correcting a power setting that had briefly carried the deviation to about 12 knots above the computed value. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to anticipate the power reduction earlier at the configuration change.
texts_at.3: SP flew the final approach speed within about 8 knots of the computed value, correcting a brief high power setting carried through the configuration change. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point, and SP is expected to anticipate the reduction earlier so the margin below 10 knots grows further.

The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent power management on final.

error_modes.label: Glide path tracking on final
error_modes.source: specific:Deviation from the desired glide path (feet)

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate monitoring of the descent rate after the configuration change, did not track the desired glide path. Deviation exceeded 300 feet above the glide path and subsequently passed 200 feet below it with an increasing sink rate, and the IP intervened with power to arrest the descent. SP did not recognize the divergence until it was called from the front cockpit.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted cross-check between the aiming point and the vertical speed, allowed the aircraft to reach the +300 foot boundary of the glide path tolerance. SP corrected only after being told the aircraft was high, and the descent back to the desired glide path was slow and continued inside 2 NM. The approach was recovered without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction at the start of the descent, allowed the aircraft to climb between 150 and 300 feet above the desired glide path. SP detected the deviation during the cross-check, applied a measured power and pitch correction and re-established the glide path well before short final, remaining inside the code 1 boundary. No IP action was required.
texts.3: SP tracked the desired glide path within 150 feet for the whole of the final segment. SP maintained an active cross-check of the aiming point against the vertical speed and made small, timely power corrections. The aircraft arrived at the threshold on the desired glide path.
texts.4: SP established the desired glide path at the configuration point and held it with negligible vertical deviation to the threshold. Corrections were anticipatory and confined to small power adjustments, with no visible excursion above or below the glide path. The vertical profile was maintained without any prompting.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the glide path standards, but the aircraft was habitually on the high side of the desired glide path and was recovered by a steeper descent inside 2 NM. The trend is a delayed initial power reduction that leaves the correction to be made low on the approach. SP is expected to start the descent at the planned point so that the glide path is established rather than regained.

texts_at.0: SP tracked the glide path on final, with the IP talking through each step as it was flown, the supporting technique still being built at this point. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage, and SP is expected to rely less on the IP's assistance as the item is repeated.

texts_at.2: SP tracked the desired glide path inside the code 2 band, correcting an excursion of about 220 feet above it that followed a late power reduction. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to begin the power reduction as soon as the descent starts rather than part-way through it.
texts_at.3: SP tracked the desired glide path within about 130 feet for the final segment, correcting a brief high excursion that followed a slightly late power reduction. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to anticipate the power reduction so the profile needs no later correction.

error_modes.label: Runway centerline alignment distance
error_modes.source: specific:Distance at which SP must be aligned with the runway center line

texts.0: SP, due to an unassessed intercept angle and no allowance for the crosswind, did not align the aircraft with the runway centerline within the required distance. The aircraft was still displaced laterally inside 1/2 NM from the threshold, and the IP had to take control inputs to place the aircraft on the extended centerline. The lateral correction was still in progress at the point where the approach had to be established.
texts.1: SP, due to a late recognition of the drift, achieved alignment with the runway centerline only at about 1/2 NM from the threshold, at the limit of the criteria. SP applied the drift correction after being prompted from the front cockpit, and the final part of the approach was flown with residual lateral corrections. No control input by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially shallow intercept of the extended centerline, completed the alignment later than briefed, between 1 1/2 and 1/2 NM from the threshold. SP recognized the lateral displacement without prompting, increased the correction and stabilized the aircraft on the centerline in time for the remainder of the approach. No IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP aligned the aircraft with the runway centerline by 1 1/2 NM from the threshold and held that alignment for the rest of the approach. SP set the drift correction early and the lateral track required only minor adjustment thereafter. The aircraft remained on the extended centerline through short final.
texts.4: SP intercepted the extended runway centerline well before 1 1/2 NM and held it with negligible lateral deviation to the threshold. The drift correction was established at the first assessment of the crosswind and needed no significant change afterwards. Lateral tracking was precise throughout the approach without any prompting.
texts.marginal: SP met the alignment distance criterion, but the alignment was completed close to the limit on each approach and was followed by small lateral corrections on short final. The tendency is to intercept the extended centerline at too shallow an angle and to under-assess the crosswind on the first assessment. SP is expected to establish the drift correction earlier so that the aircraft is stable on the centerline well before 1 1/2 NM.

Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to increase the intercept angle earlier so the drift correction is set sooner.
texts_at.3: SP aligned the aircraft with the runway centerline by about 1 1/2 NM from the threshold and held the final approach speed within about 8 knots of the computed value while the correction was made. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point, and SP is expected to set the drift correction from the first assessment of the crosswind.

error_modes.label: Approach planning to the 5 NM point on the runway extension

texts.0: SP, due to no planning of the descent and closure against the runway extension, did not bring the aircraft to five NM on the runway extension ready to configure for final. The aircraft arrived displaced from the extended centerline and well above the required profile, and the IP had to redirect the approach path and the descent to make the approach flyable. The approach was not usable as planned from that point.
texts.1: SP, due to an unplanned descent point, arrived at the five NM position off the required profile in both height and lateral track, at the limit of what the approach could absorb. SP repositioned the aircraft only after specific verbal directions from the IP, and readiness to configure was reached late. No control input by the IP was necessary.
texts.2: SP, due to a late start of the descent, approached the five NM point higher and closer to the extension than planned. SP recognized the discrepancy in time, adjusted the descent and the closure and reached the five NM position ready to configure for final without any prompting. The remainder of the approach was flown from a usable starting point.
texts.3: SP planned the approach and brought the aircraft to five NM on the runway extension, on profile and ready to configure for final. The descent and the closure were managed so that no large correction was needed at the configuration point. The approach was set up in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual.
texts.4: SP planned the approach precisely and arrived at the five NM point on the runway extension on speed, on profile and fully ready to configure for final. The lateral and vertical management of the run-in required no corrections of significance. The setup left ample capacity for the configuration and the final segment.
texts.marginal: SP arrived at the five NM point within standards, but consistently a little high and with the descent still being adjusted at the moment of configuring. The trend is to plan the descent point by reference to the runway rather than by a computed distance. SP is expected to fix the descent point during the planning so that the aircraft is stabilized at five NM before configuration begins.

texts_at.0: SP planned the approach toward the five NM point, with the IP walking through the sequence step by step, the pace of the item still unfamiliar at this point. error_modes.label: ATC clearance and clearing during the approach

texts.0: SP, due to distraction by radio traffic while established on final, did not obtain the ATC clearance in a timely manner and did not execute the required clearing during the approach. The aircraft continued the straight-in without a valid clearance and with no lookout for conflicting traffic, and the IP had to make the transmission and take over the clearing. The approach was continued only after the IP had regularized the clearance.
texts.1: SP, due to distraction by a secondary cockpit task during the run-in, requested the straight-in clearance late and performed the clearing only after the IP prompted for it. The clearance was obtained before the final segment, but the traffic scan during the approach was verbal and incomplete. No IP control input was necessary.
texts.2: SP, due to a transmission made while the configuration was still being completed, requested the clearance later than planned. SP recognized the omission, obtained the clearance without prompting and executed the clearing turns and the visual scan during the remainder of the approach. The approach continued with a valid clearance and an adequate lookout.
texts.3: SP obtained the ATC clearance for the straight-in in a timely manner and executed the required clearing during the approach. The transmissions were made at the planned points and did not interfere with the flying of the profile. The traffic scan was maintained throughout the approach.
texts.4: SP obtained the clearance early and without any interference with the flight path, and maintained an active clearing scan through every segment of the approach. Radio work was concise, standard and fitted into the low workload parts of the profile. Nothing in the communications sequence had to be prompted or repeated.
texts.marginal: SP obtained the clearance and cleared during the approach as required, but the requests were made at the same moment as the configuration changes and the visual scan narrowed while transmitting. The trend is to concentrate the radio work into the busiest part of the profile. SP is expected to sequence the transmissions before the configuration point so that the lookout is not interrupted.

error_modes.label: Descent start point from the aim point visual cue

texts.0: SP, due to starting the letdown before the aim point cue of the flown configuration appeared, left 1500 feet AGL early and did not use the threshold in the lower 1/3 of the windscreen for flaps LDG or TO, or the spinner on the threshold for flaps UP, as the reference. The early descent placed the aircraft more than 200 feet below the desired 3-4 degree glide path and the flat profile could no longer be held at the computed final approach speed. IP intervened with power and pitch to regain the glide path before the approach could be continued.
texts.1: SP, due to judging the descent point from the general runway picture instead of the prescribed aim point cue, began the descent early and let the aircraft settle to the 200 foot lower boundary of the glide path tolerance. SP added power and levelled off only after the low profile was called from the front cockpit. Distance to the threshold was not cross-checked against the descent point, and the desired glide path was regained late, without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to an imprecise reading of the aim point cue in the windscreen, started the descent slightly before the correct point and went between 150 and 200 feet below the desired glide path. SP recognized the flat profile from the movement of the aim point, added power and levelled off to intercept the 3-4 degree glide path, containing the deviation inside the code 1 boundary. The correction was made without prompting and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP left 1500 feet AGL only when the aim point cue for the flown configuration was met, the threshold in the lower 1/3 of the windscreen with flaps LDG or TO and the spinner on the threshold with flaps UP. The resulting 3-4 degree profile kept the aircraft within 150 feet of the desired glide path for the whole final. Distance to the threshold was cross-checked against the planned descent point as briefed.
texts.4: SP identified the aim point cue for the configuration flown and started the descent exactly at that point, backed up by the distance to the threshold. The 3-4 degree glide path was established from the first moment of the descent and held with negligible vertical deviation. No re-interception of the profile was needed at any stage of the straight-in.
texts.marginal: SP started the descent within standards, but consistently a little before the aim point cue appeared in the windscreen, so the aircraft was habitually on the low side and the profile had to be regained by levelling off inside 2 NM. The tendency is to judge the descent point from the runway picture alone without cross-checking the distance to the threshold. SP is expected to hold 1500 feet AGL until the cue for the flown configuration is actually met.

error_modes.label: Recognition and recovery of a low (dragged-in) final

texts.0: SP, due to not recognizing that the aircraft was below the proper glide path, held the normal power setting on a shallower than normal profile, where that setting is too low to maintain airspeed. Airspeed decayed below the computed final approach speed, which the one-sided tolerance does not permit at all, and the aircraft passed more than 200 feet below the desired glide path with an increasing sink rate. SP neither added power and levelled off nor went around, and the IP intervened with power to recover the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving power at the normal setting after the glide path had shallowed, allowed the aircraft to reach the 200 foot lower limit of the tolerance with the airspeed decaying toward the computed value. SP added power and levelled off to intercept the proper glide path only after the low approach was called from the front cockpit. The recovery was completed without IP control input, but the decision to correct came from instruction.
texts.2: SP, due to a normal power setting carried onto a slightly flat profile, went between 150 and 200 feet below the desired glide path with the airspeed beginning to decay. SP recognized the dragged-in condition, added power, levelled off and intercepted the proper glide path in time, keeping the deviation inside the code 1 boundary and the speed at the computed value. No prompting or IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP recognized any tendency to go below the proper glide path early and corrected it with a timely power addition and a level-off to intercept the desired profile. Vertical deviation stayed within 150 feet and the computed final approach airspeed was maintained throughout. The aircraft was never allowed to develop a dragged-in final.
texts.4: SP matched power to the actual glide path continuously, so the aircraft never settled below the desired profile and no recovery action was needed. Vertical deviation was negligible and the airspeed stayed at the computed value with a stable sink rate. The go around decision point for a too low or too slow approach was set and stated in advance.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the glide path and airspeed standards, but the aircraft repeatedly drifted to the low side of the profile and was recovered by adding power late on the approach. The trend is not to increase power when the glide path shallows, where the normal setting can no longer hold the airspeed. SP is expected to correct power as soon as the profile flattens, so that a dragged-in final never develops.

error_modes.label: Flap configuration selection against landing distance, crosswind and gusts

texts.0: SP, due to not assessing the crosswind, the gust and the required landing distance against the runway length, selected a configuration the manual excludes for the conditions, planning flaps LDG with a crosswind above the 10 KIAS training limit and in gusty wind. SP did not consider flaps TO, which the manual prescribes for crosswinds of 10 knots or greater. IP directed a change of configuration and the approach had to be re-planned, with the final airspeed outside the criteria while the change was being made.
texts.1: SP, due to a superficial assessment of the reported wind, planned the straight-in with flaps LDG although the crosswind was at the 10 KIAS training limit, and changed to flaps TO only after being questioned from the front cockpit. The late change compressed the configuration sequence and the final airspeed reached the +15 knot limit of the tolerance before the correct target was re-established. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to weighing the landing distance before the crosswind and the gust, hesitated between flaps LDG and flaps TO and fixed the configuration later than briefed. SP reassessed the reported conditions in time, selected the configuration the manual prescribes and flew its final airspeed, containing the deviation to about 12 knots above the computed value. The decision was reached without prompting from the IP.
texts.3: SP selected the flap configuration from the actual conditions, using flaps LDG when the landing distance was equal to or greater than 80 percent of the runway length and flaps TO for crosswinds of 10 knots or greater. The base turn and final airspeeds flown were those of the selected configuration and stayed within +10, -0 knots. The choice was briefed and needed no change during the approach.
texts.4: SP assessed runway length, required landing distance, crosswind and gust before the approach and selected the configuration the manual prescribes, respecting the 10 KIAS training crosswind limit for flaps LDG. The corresponding final approach speed was established at once and held with negligible deviation. The configuration was fixed early enough that no re-planning was needed at the configuration point.
texts.marginal: SP selected an acceptable configuration on each approach, but the choice was made close to the configuration point and only after the wind had been read a second time. The tendency is to default to the configuration flown on the previous approach instead of deriving it from landing distance, crosswind and gust. SP is expected to fix the configuration during the planning to the five NM point.

texts_at.0: SP worked the flap configuration selection for wind and distance, with the IP demonstrating the technique first, a first exposure to this task at this stage of the syllabus. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard, and SP is expected to carry more of the task independently at the next opportunity.

texts_at.3: SP selected the flap configuration from the actual conditions and flew its final airspeed within about 8 knots of the computed value. error_modes.label: Gust correction on final approach and touchdown speeds

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the gust correction in gusty wind, did not add one-half of the gust to the final approach and touchdown speeds and flew the plain computed value. Airspeed fell below the computed final approach speed in the lulls, which the one-sided tolerance does not permit at all, and the approach became unstable in pitch and power. IP took control inputs to restore the speed before the threshold.
texts.1: SP, due to applying the gust correction from the previous approach instead of the actual reported gust, added more than one-half of the gust and exceeded the 10 KIAS maximum. Final approach speed sat at the +15 knot limit of the tolerance until the IP called for it to be reduced. The corrected target was re-established late on final, without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a late reading of the reported gust, applied the correction only after configuring and briefly carried more than +10 knots over the computed final approach speed. SP recomputed one-half of the gust, capped it at 10 KIAS and settled the speed inside the code 1 boundary before short final. The correction was made without prompting and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP added one-half of the gust, up to the maximum of 10 KIAS, to the final approach and touchdown speeds and flew that corrected target throughout. Airspeed stayed within +10, -0 knots of the target and never decayed below it in the lulls. The correction was computed before the configuration point as briefed.
texts.4: SP derived the correction from the actual reported gust, applied exactly one-half of it within the 10 KIAS maximum and established the corrected speed immediately after configuring. Deviations from the corrected target were negligible through the gusts and the touchdown speed carried the same correction. No further adjustment was needed after the initial power setting.
texts.marginal: SP applied a gust correction that kept the speed within standards, but the amount was rounded upward and the airspeed sat habitually near the top of the tolerance. The trend is to treat the correction as a fixed additive rather than one-half of the actual gust up to 10 KIAS. SP is expected to recompute it from the reported gust on each approach.

texts_at.0: SP applied the gust correction on final approach, with the IP talking through each step as it was flown, the supporting technique still being built at this point. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage, and SP is expected to rely less on the IP's assistance as the item is repeated.
texts_at.1: SP applied the gust correction within the code 1 band, the final approach speed sitting about 14 knots above the computed value until the corrected target was re-established. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to compute one-half of the reported gust before the configuration point rather than after it.
texts_at.2: SP applied the gust correction within the code 2 band, the final approach speed running about 12 knots above the computed value before it settled inside the tolerance. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to read the reported gust earlier so the correction is applied before configuring rather than after.
texts_at.3: SP added one-half of the gust to the final approach speed and held the corrected target within about 8 knots throughout. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to recompute the correction from the actual reported gust on every approach rather than carrying it from the previous one.

error_modes.label: Airspeed cross-check against the ON-SPEED AOA indication

texts.0: SP, due to flying the configuration airspeed on the airspeed indicator alone with no AOA cross-check, allowed the aircraft to become slower than the ON-SPEED AOA indication during the approach. Airspeed went below the computed final approach speed, which the criteria do not permit at all, and the aircraft was on the low side of the glide path with a rising sink rate. IP added power and intervened before SP had begun to recover the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to dropping the AOA from the cross-check at the configuration change, let the indexer move toward the slow indication and the airspeed fall to the computed value with no margin left. SP added power to re-establish the ON-SPEED indication only after being prompted from the front cockpit. The remainder of the approach was flown at the computed speed without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to an interrupted AOA cross-check while completing the configuration, diverged from the ON-SPEED indication and the airspeed moved through the upper part of the tolerance before it settled. SP restored the cross-check, matched power to the indexer and held the computed final approach speed to about 12 knots above the computed value for the rest of the approach. No prompting or IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP cross-checked airspeed against AOA throughout the approach and at no point flew slower than the ON-SPEED AOA indication. The computed final approach airspeed of the selected configuration was maintained within +10, -0 knots. Power was adjusted to keep the indexer on speed at each configuration change.
texts.4: SP flew the approach with a continuous airspeed and AOA cross-check and held the ON-SPEED indication with negligible movement of the indexer. The computed final approach speed of the configuration was matched exactly and the slow side was never approached. Power corrections were anticipatory and no divergence between the two references developed.
texts.marginal: SP never flew slower than the ON-SPEED AOA indication, but the indexer was habitually allowed to drift toward the slow side before power was added. The trend is to fly the approach on the airspeed indicator and to consult the AOA only once a deviation is felt. SP is expected to keep the AOA in the cross-check so that the ON-SPEED indication is maintained rather than recovered.

texts_at.1: SP cross-checked airspeed against AOA within the code 1 band, the final approach speed running about 14 knots above the computed value before the indexer was returned to the ON-SPEED indication. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to keep the AOA in the cross-check continuously rather than consulting it only after a deviation is felt.
texts_at.2: SP cross-checked airspeed against AOA within the code 2 band, the final approach speed running about 12 knots above the computed value before power was matched to the indexer again. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to restore the AOA cross-check as soon as the configuration change is complete.
texts_at.3: SP cross-checked airspeed against AOA and held the final approach speed within about 8 knots of the computed value throughout. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point, and SP is expected to keep the cross-check continuous through every configuration change rather than only after it.

The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.

error_modes.label: Final airspeed matched to the selected flap setting

texts.0: SP, due to carrying over the target of the previously flown configuration, flew the straight-in at a final approach speed that does not belong to the selected flap setting, holding the flaps LDG value of 100 KIAS with flaps UP where 110 KIAS is required. The speed was therefore below the computed value for the configuration flown, which the one-sided tolerance does not permit, and the aircraft was near the slow side with a high pitch attitude. IP directed and then applied the power correction to restore the correct target.
texts.1: SP, due to not restating the target after the flap setting was changed, flew the final about ten knots fast for the selected configuration and reached the +15 knot limit of the tolerance. SP set the correct configuration speed, 100 KIAS with flaps LDG, 105 KIAS with flaps TO or 110 KIAS with flaps UP, only after the IP stated the required value. The rest of the final was flown on the correct target, without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed recall of the airspeed belonging to the selected flap setting, initially flew a target more than 10 knots above the correct final approach speed. SP corrected the target from the configuration actually flown, reduced power and re-established the correct speed well before short final, keeping the deviation short of the code 1 boundary. No prompting or IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP flew the final approach speed of the selected configuration, 100 KIAS with flaps LDG, 105 KIAS with flaps TO and 110 KIAS with flaps UP, and held it within +10, -0 knots. The target was restated at the configuration change and power was set directly to it. The straight-in was flown on speed for the whole final segment.
texts.4: SP identified the final approach speed of the selected flap setting before configuring and established it immediately after the configuration was complete. Deviation from that target was negligible to the threshold and the speed never went below the value for the configuration flown. Successive approaches with different flap settings were flown on their own targets without any prompting.
texts.marginal: SP flew the correct target for each flap setting, but the value was recalled late and the first approach after a change of configuration was flown a few knots off before it was trimmed on. The trend is to keep the airspeed of the previous approach until the deviation becomes visible. SP is expected to state the final approach speed of the selected configuration before configuring.

texts_at.0: SP matched the final airspeed to the flap setting, with the IP walking through the sequence step by step, the pace of the item still unfamiliar at this point. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recall the configuration speed sooner after each flap change.
texts_at.3: SP flew the final approach speed of the selected configuration and held it within about 8 knots throughout. texts_above.2: SP recognized a delayed recall of the airspeed belonging to the selected flap setting and corrected the target, holding the final approach speed to about 12 knots off the correct value well before short final. error_modes.label: Descent from 1500 ft AGL: arrival at the 2 NM point high, so the configuration and the slow-down are stacked on final
error_modes.source: specific:Deviation from the desired glide path (feet)|specific:AIRSPEED (knots) / FINAL|general:a,b

texts.0: SP, due to leaving 1500 ft AGL well inside the 5 NM point with the power still at the cruise setting, arrived at the 2 NM point more than 300 ft above the desired glide path with the configuration not started. The gear and the flaps were selected on a steep, idle-power final and the airspeed was still more than 15 kt above the final approach speed on short final, with the result that the approach could not be stabilized. The IP called the go-around.
texts.1: SP, due to a descent started late from the 5 NM point, arrived at the 2 NM point 300 ft above the desired glide path, at the limit of the tolerance, with the result that the configuration and the slow-down were made together on a steep final and the airspeed settled 15 kt above the final approach speed, at the limit, on short final. SP reduced the power to idle only after the IP called the energy. The approach was stabilized on short final.
texts.2: SP, due to a descent rate a little shallower than the distance to the 2 NM point required, arrived at the configuration point about 220 ft above the desired glide path, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, with the result that the final approach speed was reached late and the airspeed was about 12 kt fast approaching short final.
